objections.response: That's fair to raise, and I'd rather talk about it now than at the end. Can we look at it against what the problem costs you today? When teams add up the hours, the tools they'd retire, and the risk they carry, the comparison usually looks very different from list price alone.
talkingPoints: Anchor on the cost of the problem, not the price of the product
Total cost of ownership includes people, maintenance, and tools retired
Phased rollouts let you prove value before scaling spend
questions: Expensive compared to what — another vendor, or the budget you have?
What would solving this be worth to the business this year?
If price were equal, which option would you choose?

objections.objection: We already have a tool that does this.
objections.response: Makes sense — most teams we talk to do. The question is whether it's delivering what you need. Many customers run {{product}} alongside what they have and start with the use case where the current tool falls short. What's the gap that made this conversation worth having?
talkingPoints: Coexist first, consolidate later — no rip-and-replace required
Focus on the gap, not a feature-by-feature bake-off
Retiring overlapping tools often funds the change
questions: What does your current tool do well?
Where do people work around it today?
When does that contract renew?

objections.response: Understood — timing matters. Can I ask what would make it the right time? Often the cost of waiting is higher than it looks, especially if the problem compounds every quarter. If it's a resourcing question, we can scope a first phase that fits around what you have on your plate.
talkingPoints: Quantify the cost of waiting per month or quarter
Tie back to deadlines and initiatives they already mentioned
Offer a smaller first phase that fits current capacity
questions: What's competing for priority right now?
What happens if this waits six months?
What would need to be true to start next quarter?

objections.response: You probably could — you clearly have a strong team. The question is whether this is the best use of them. Building the first version is the easy part; maintaining, securing, and scaling it for years is where the cost hides. Most teams would rather put those engineers on the work that differentiates your business.
talkingPoints: Build cost is the tip of the iceberg; maintenance is the rest
Opportunity cost: engineers on core product versus internal tooling
Time to value: weeks with {{product}} versus quarters to build
questions: Have you scoped what it would take to build and maintain?
Who would own it long term?
What would that team work on otherwise?

objections.response: That's a common worry, usually based on past projects. We scope to a first use case that goes live quickly, then expand. I can walk you through a typical rollout plan for a team your size, and put you in touch with a customer who's been through it.
talkingPoints: Start with one high-value use case and a clear go-live date
A proven implementation playbook and named owners on our side
Customer references with similar scope and timelines
questions: What was your experience with past implementations?
How much time can your team commit each week?
What date would make this a success?

objections.objection: Our team won't adopt another tool.
objections.response: Adoption is the whole game, so I'm glad you raised it. We see strong adoption when the tool fits into how people already work and makes their day easier on day one. Let's identify the group that feels the most pain — they tend to become the champions.
talkingPoints: Meet users where they work with integrations and familiar workflows
Enablement and success resources included, not extra
Start with the most motivated team and let results spread
questions: Which past rollouts went well, and why?
Who would be the first team to benefit?
What would make this easier than what they do today?

objections.objection: We need to get IT and security involved first.
objections.response: Absolutely — and the earlier the better. We can share our security documentation and completed questionnaires now so review runs in parallel rather than at the end. Who's the right person on that team to connect with?
talkingPoints: Security package ready to share: certifications, questionnaires, architecture
Run security review in parallel with the business evaluation
Offer a technical session with their architects
questions: What does your security review process look like?
Are there requirements that are typically deal-breakers?
Can we get time with them this week or next?

objections.response: Happy to. So I send you something useful rather than a generic deck, can I ask two quick questions about what you're trying to solve? Then I'll tailor it and suggest a short follow-up once you've had a look.
talkingPoints: Earn two minutes of discovery before sending anything
Tailored material beats a generic deck
Always leave with a next step on the calendar
questions: What would make this worth another conversation?
Who else should see what I send?
Can we pencil in 20 minutes next week to go through it?

objections.objection: We're locked into a contract with another vendor.
objections.response: That's helpful to know. When does it renew? Teams often use the months before renewal to validate an alternative, so they have leverage and a clear plan instead of an automatic renewal. We can also start in an area your current contract doesn't cover.
talkingPoints: Use the renewal window to evaluate with no switching pressure
Start with an adjacent use case outside the existing contract
Build the business case now so the decision is ready at renewal
questions: When is the renewal date, and when does the notice period start?
How happy is the team with the current vendor?
Who decides whether to renew?

objections.objection: We don't have the budget this year.
objections.response: Understood. Budget usually follows priorities — if the business case is strong enough, where would the money typically come from? Some customers fund this by retiring existing tools, others start small this year and expand next budget cycle.
talkingPoints: Find the budget owner and the business case they need
Tools retired and hours saved can self-fund the change
Phased commercial options to match the budget cycle
questions: When does your next budget cycle start?
Who would need to sponsor this for budget to appear?
What existing spend overlaps with this?

objections.objection: You're too small / we haven't heard of you.
objections.response: Fair question — you should know who you're betting on. I can share who else in your industry uses {{product}}, how we support customers, and our roadmap. Many customers find they get more attention and influence working with us than they would with a larger vendor.
talkingPoints: Relevant customer references and case studies
Clear support model and named contacts
Customer influence on the roadmap
questions: What would you need to see to feel confident?
Would a reference call with a similar customer help?
What has your experience been with larger vendors?

objections.objection: It's missing a feature we need.
objections.response: Thanks for being direct. Can you tell me more about how you'd use that feature? Sometimes there's another way to get the same outcome, and if it's truly a gap I'd rather tell you honestly and show you where it sits on the roadmap.
talkingPoints: Dig into the outcome behind the feature request
Show alternatives and workarounds that meet the need
Be honest about gaps and roadmap timing
questions: What outcome does that feature give you?
How often would you use it?
Is it a must-have for day one, or for later?
